chapters.title: Chapter 1: What You Actually Own in a Startup

lessons.title: Authorised, Issued and Fully Diluted Share Capital

children.text: A founder sends you a one-line offer: "The company has 1,00,000 shares. We will issue you 5,000 shares for ₹5 lakh. That is 5%." Every number in that sentence can be true and you can still end up owning closer to 4%. The gap comes from which share count you divide by. This lesson shows you the three share counts every Indian company has and teaches you to insist on the one that matters.

body.text: Your ownership is only as real as the denominator behind it. Always ask for the fully diluted share count, because it includes every share that exists today and every share that has already been promised to someone else.

children.text: Three Layers of Share Capital

Think of a company's share capital as three nested boxes. The outer box is the legal ceiling. The middle box is what has actually been handed out. The inner reality, the one investors care about, adds everything that will be handed out if existing promises are kept.

body.caption: The three share counts you will see in startup documents

cells: The maximum share capital the company is allowed to issue
Capital clause of the Memorandum of Association
A ceiling, not ownership. Tells you whether new shares can be issued without a shareholder vote
Shares actually allotted to shareholders, equity and preference
Return of allotment (Form PAS-3), annual return (Form MGT-7), register of members
Issued shares plus every share that could come into existence: ESOP pool, conversion of preference shares and notes, warrants
The cap table shared by the company, and the term sheet
The only honest base for calculating your percentage

children.text: Authorised capital: the ceiling
When a company is incorporated, its
Memorandum of Association
states its
authorised capital

, for example "₹3,00,000 divided into 2,00,000 equity shares of ₹1 each and 10,000 preference shares of ₹10 each". The company cannot issue a share beyond this limit. Authorised capital tells you nothing about who owns what. It only tells you how much room is left.

markDefs.definition: The charter document filed at incorporation that states the company's name, registered office, objects and authorised share capital.
The maximum amount of share capital, at face value, that a company is permitted to issue under its Memorandum of Association.

body.title: How a company raises its authorised capital

children.text: If a funding round needs more shares than the ceiling allows, the company must first increase its authorised capital:
Check the Articles.
Section 61 of the Companies Act, 2013 allows the increase if the Articles of Association permit it.
Pass a shareholder resolution.
An ordinary resolution is the default, unless the Articles demand a special resolution.
Alter the Memorandum.
The capital clause is updated to the new figure.
File with the Registrar of Companies.
Form SH-7 is filed within 30 days, along with the government fee and stamp duty on the increase.
For an investor, this step is a small signal. If a round is closing and nobody has increased the authorised capital, the paperwork is behind schedule.
Issued capital: what exists today
Issued capital

is the shares the company has actually allotted, to founders, angels, funds and anyone else. In startups, shares are almost always fully paid at allotment, so you will see "issued", "subscribed" and "paid-up" used interchangeably. Issued capital includes both equity shares and preference shares such as CCPS.

markDefs.definition: Shares actually allotted by the company. In startups these are almost always fully paid, so issued, subscribed and paid-up capital are usually the same number.

children.text: Fully diluted capital: what will exist
Several instruments are promises of future shares. They are not shares yet, but each one will become shares if a condition is met. The
fully diluted
count assumes all of them already have.

markDefs.definition: A share count that assumes every option, warrant, convertible preference share and convertible note has already turned into equity shares.

children.text: ESOP pool.
Shares reserved for employee stock options, both options already granted and those not yet allocated to anyone.
CCPS.
Compulsorily convertible preference shares that will turn into equity shares at a set ratio. Lesson 1.3 covers them.
Convertible notes and iSAFEs.
Money already received that will convert into shares at a future round. Lesson 3.4 covers the mechanics.
Warrants.
Rights to buy shares at a fixed price, often given to venture debt lenders alongside a loan.

body.latex: \text{Fully diluted shares} = \text{Issued equity} + \text{CCPS on conversion} + \text{ESOP pool} + \text{Warrants} + \text{Convertibles}
body.caption: Count every share that has been promised, not just the ones already allotted

body.text: The unallocated part of the ESOP pool counts. Founders sometimes argue that options not yet granted to anyone should be ignored. They should not. The company has reserved those shares specifically to hand out, and when it does, your percentage falls.

children.text: Worked Example: The TiffinBox Offer
TiffinBox Foods Private Limited is a fictional Hyderabad startup delivering home-style lunches to office workers. Here is how its share capital was built up before it offered you shares.

events.title: Incorporation
events.description: Authorised capital of ₹3,00,000: 2,00,000 equity shares of ₹1 and 10,000 preference shares of ₹10. Co-founders Ravi and Sana take 45,000 and 30,000 equity shares.

events.title: Angel round
events.description: A group of angels is allotted 15,000 equity shares.

events.title: Seed fund invests
events.description: A seed fund is allotted 10,000 CCPS, each converting into 1 equity share.

events.title: ESOP scheme approved
events.description: Shareholders approve a pool of 12,000 options by special resolution. 4,000 are granted to early employees and 8,000 remain unallocated.

events.title: Venture debt
events.description: A venture debt lender provides a working capital loan and receives warrants for 5,000 equity shares.

events.title: Your offer
events.description: 5,000 new equity shares at ₹100 each, for ₹5 lakh.

children.text: Now calculate your stake three ways.

body.caption: Same 5,000 shares, three different answers
headers: Implied company value at ₹100 per share

body.title: Show me how the fully diluted count is built

children.text: Equity shares: Ravi 45,000 + Sana 30,000 + angels 15,000 = 90,000
CCPS on conversion: 10,000 × 1 = 10,000
Issued capital before your round: 90,000 + 10,000 = 1,00,000
ESOP pool, granted and unallocated: 12,000
Warrants: 5,000
Fully diluted before your round: 1,00,000 + 12,000 + 5,000 = 1,17,000
Your new shares: 5,000
Fully diluted after your round: 1,17,000 + 5,000 = 1,22,000

body.title: Your ownership depends on the denominator

children.text: The founder's 5% made two mistakes. It divided by a share count that did not include your own new shares, and it ignored 17,000 promised shares. The effect on price is just as important. You believed you were paying ₹5 lakh for 5% of a ₹1 crore company. On a fully diluted basis you are paying the same ₹5 lakh for 4.10% of a ₹1.22 crore company, a valuation 22% higher than the pitch.

body.title: TiffinBox fully diluted ownership after your round (shares)
Ravi's real stake
body.prompt: Ravi holds 45,000 equity shares. After your round, what is his fully diluted ownership of TiffinBox? Give your answer as a percentage to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 45,000 ÷ 1,22,000 = 36.9%. On an issued basis after your round he would appear to own 45,000 ÷ 1,05,000 = 42.9%. The six-point gap is the ESOP pool and warrants, which is exactly why founders and investors negotiate on a fully diluted basis.

body.text: Check the headroom too. After your round, TiffinBox's equity shares on a fully diluted basis total 1,22,000 (including 10,000 from CCPS conversion), comfortably within the 2,00,000 authorised equity shares. But all 10,000 authorised preference shares are already issued. If the Series A investor wants CCPS, which is the norm in India, the company must first increase its authorised capital.

children.text: Why Fully Diluted Is the Industry Standard

Term sheets from Indian angel networks and VC funds state ownership "on a fully diluted basis" for exactly the reason you just saw. Listed companies follow the same logic: offer documents for new-age IPOs filed with SEBI typically show pre-issue shareholding on a fully diluted basis, so that outstanding employee options are not hidden from public investors.

body.label: Typical ESOP pool size
body.context: A commonly seen range for Indian startups from seed to Series B. It varies widely, and investors often ask for the pool to be created or topped up before they invest. Lesson 3.3 explains why that timing matters.

body.title: Issued basis vs fully diluted basis

columns.label: Issued basis
points: Useful for legal questions such as who can vote today
Can overstate what a new investor will own

columns.label: Fully diluted basis
points: Counts issued shares plus every promised share
Shows the smallest, most realistic stake
Used for pricing, valuation and negotiations
The basis to insist on before you sign

body.title: What belongs in issued capital?
body.question: Which of these is counted in fully diluted capital but NOT in issued capital?
options: Equity shares allotted to the founders
CCPS already allotted to a seed fund
ESOP options reserved in the pool but not yet granted
Equity shares allotted to angel investors
body.explanation: Options, whether granted or not, are not shares until they are exercised, so they sit outside issued capital. CCPS are already allotted preference shares, so they are part of issued capital today and simply convert into equity later.

body.title: The ceiling
body.textWithBlank: The maximum share capital a company may issue, as stated in its Memorandum of Association, is called its ___ capital.
body.explanation: Authorised capital is a legal ceiling, not a measure of ownership. Raising it needs a shareholder resolution and a Form SH-7 filing.

children.text: Before You Sign: Your Share Count Checklist

body.title: Ask for these before you invest
steps: Get the full cap table on a fully diluted basis, both before and after the round.
Confirm the size of the ESOP pool, and how much of it is granted versus unallocated.
List every CCPS series and its conversion ratio.
List every convertible note, iSAFE and warrant, with the number of shares each is expected to become.
Check whether the ESOP pool is being created or enlarged as part of this round.
Confirm there is enough authorised capital for your shares and for every conversion.
Recalculate your percentage yourself: your shares divided by the post-round fully diluted count.

body.title: "Founders own 75%"
body.scenario: A pitch deck from a Bengaluru SaaS startup says: "Founders own 75% of the company." In the data room, you find the company has 75,000 founder equity shares, 25,000 CCPS held by investors, a 15,000-share ESOP pool and warrants for 5,000 shares.
body.prompt: Is the 75% claim wrong? What is the founders' fully diluted ownership, and what would you ask the founders?
body.modelAnswer:
The claim is technically true, but it uses a flattering denominator. Issued capital is 75,000 + 25,000 = 1,00,000 shares, and 75,000 of 1,00,000 is 75%.

Fully diluted capital is 1,00,000 + 15,000 + 5,000 = 1,20,000 shares. Founders own 75,000 ÷ 1,20,000 = 62.5%. The deck overstates their real stake by 12.5 percentage points.

Questions to ask:
1. Can you restate the deck on a fully diluted basis?
2. Is the ESOP pool fully disclosed, including any top-up planned for this round?
3. Are there any other convertible notes, iSAFEs or warrants outstanding?
4. Can you share the cap table on a fully diluted basis, before and after this round?

cards.definition: The legal ceiling on share capital a company may issue, stated in its Memorandum of Association.
Shares actually allotted to shareholders, both equity and preference. In startups, usually the same as paid-up capital.
Issued shares plus every share that could come into existence through ESOPs, conversions and warrants.
Shares reserved for employee stock options, including options not yet granted to anyone.
A right to buy shares at a fixed price, often issued to venture debt lenders.
The Registrar of Companies filing made within 30 days of increasing authorised capital.
The return of allotment filed with the Registrar of Companies after a company issues new shares.

points: Authorised capital is a ceiling, issued capital is what exists today, and fully diluted capital is what will exist once every promise is kept.
Fully diluted capital includes the whole ESOP pool, CCPS on conversion, convertible notes and warrants.
The same number of shares can look like 5% or 4.10% depending on the denominator.
A smaller denominator also hides a higher valuation: paying the same amount for a smaller real stake means paying a higher price.
Indian term sheets state ownership on a fully diluted basis. Insist on it and recalculate your stake yourself.
Check that authorised capital has room for your shares and all future conversions.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. TiffinBox and the SaaS startup in the exercise are fictional. Startup investments are high risk, illiquid and can result in the loss of your entire capital. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser and a qualified legal professional before investing.
